headline: Your bone age
subhead: IS MEASURED FROM THE WRONG BONES

headline: Bone age
body: So when someone tells you your bone age, that number came from an X-ray of your **hand and wrist**. One picture, one number, and then that number gets used to guess how much growing your legs have left. | The problem is that your hand is not where your height comes from, and as we will see, it is not even on the same schedule.
punch: ==Your hand is not where your height comes from.==

headline: The first study
body: This one looked at how different bones in the same animal stop growing. In mice, *epiphyseal fusion*, which is the growth plate disappearing for good, happened at about **3 weeks** in the finger bones and **4 weeks** in the metacarpals. | The tibia and femur? Still open at **12 weeks**. Same mouse, same genes, completely different clocks.
punch: _The finger bones close while the leg bones are barely started._

headline: Same thing in rats
body: Now you might think that is a mouse quirk. So they did it in rats too: **12 weeks** in the phalanges, **16 weeks** in the metacarpals, and the tibias and femurs still open at 16. | Two species, same pattern. The small bones always go first.
punch: This is not a quirk of one animal.

headline: And it's not just timing
body: The same study measured how fast each bone was actually growing. At one week old, the metacarpal was growing at **49%** of the tibial rate, and the number of cell divisions per column in its growth plate was **46%** of the tibia's. | So the hand bones are not just finishing earlier, they are running slower the whole way.
punch: ==Your hand bones grow at half the speed of your legs.==

headline: Why? They age faster
body: Every marker of *growth plate senescence*, which is the plate slowly running out of cell divisions, was further along in the metacarpals and phalanges than in the femurs and tibias at the same age. | What this means is that all your bones are on the same curve, but the small ones are further down it at any given moment.
punch: _Different bones. Same curve. Different positions on it._

headline: The reason
body: This is the part I found most interesting. They took *chondrocytes*, the cells that build the growth plate, out of finger bones and out of leg bones. The finger cells divided slower. | Then they added IGF-1 to the finger cells, and their proliferation rose **to match the untreated leg cells**. So the difference is not the bone itself, it is how much growth signal is reaching it.
punch: The bone is the same. The signal is not.

headline: You can see it
body: In the tibia and femur, cell division extended **farther down the columns** of the growth plate than in the metacarpals and phalanges. More of the plate is still working. | That is what a younger plate looks like under a microscope, and the leg bones have it when the hand bones do not.
punch: Longer bones keep more of their plate working.

headline: So a hand X-ray
body: Put that together. The hand is the part of you that is furthest through the process, and it is being used to estimate the part with the most left. | Those are two different measurements, and the second one is the one you actually care about.
punch: ==You are measuring the finished work to guess at the unfinished.==

headline: The second study
body: Now lets move to humans. Kvist 2021 did MRI on **958 people** aged 14 to 21, imaging the wrist, the knee and the ankle in the same person. | They found that fusion timing varied by site inside one body, and that complete fusion happened about **2 years earlier** in girls than boys.

headline: And they checked
body: *Pubertal stage*, meaning where you are in puberty rather than how old you are, correlated with fusion at every site they imaged. Wrist **0.596**, upper shin **0.597**, ankle **0.598**, heel **0.514** in males. | Females lower but present, 0.287 to 0.513.
punch: Your puberty stage is the variable to track.

headline: Then two more things
body: **BMI correlated** with growth plate maturity, 0.186 to 0.384, higher in males. | **Physical activity** had no significant correlation in males at any site. In females there was one very low correlation at the wrist, **0.095**, and nothing else. | So the study found that being heavier tracked faster maturation, and training barely registered.
punch: ==Being heavier tracked faster maturation. Training barely registered.==

headline: Which is worth
body: Because most height advice you will see is about training. And in the largest human imaging study we have on this, activity did not move growth plate maturity in any meaningful way. Body composition did. | That does not mean training is bad. It means training is not what is spending your plates.
punch: _Training is not what is spending your plates._

headline: So how do we use this?
body: Treat it as an estimate from your fastest-ageing bones, not a readout of your legs. Track your *pubertal stage*, because that tracked fusion at every site the study imaged. | And remember the order: the hand finishes first, always.
